notes: Complete adjourned sentencing appeal; s.37 MHA hospital order requirements clearly decided.

enrichment.short_title: Adjourned appeal where s.37 hospital order lacked current medical evidence
key_facts: The appellant was convicted at Lewes Crown Court of making a threat to kill and sentenced to detention in hospital under section 37 of the Mental Health Act 1983.
In June 2001 he threatened to kill PC Chaffey; he had prior obsessions with police and a January 2001 probation for assault on a police officer.
Medical reports from Dr Stamps and Dr Warsi described depression and paranoid features, but Dr Warsi had not seen the appellant since June 2000 and said a full hospital assessment was needed.
The court held the section 37 requirements were not satisfied on the evidence before the Recorder, particularly because up-to-date medical evidence was lacking.
Counsel sought immediate release after 190 days in custody, but the court adjourned the appeal for fresh section 12 medical reports and a probation report on community rehabilitation alternatives.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeal with leave against a Crown Court section 37 hospital order; appeal adjourned part-heard for further medical and probation reports.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal adjourned; directions for two registered medical practitioner reports within 28 days, probation report, extended legal aid, and relisting before 14 August 2003.
enrichment.ratio: A section 37 hospital order requires up-to-date written or oral evidence from at least two registered medical practitioners (one section 12 approved) as to the offender's current mental condition and susceptibility to treatment at sentencing; stale or inadequate medical evidence cannot satisfy the statutory conditions.
legal_issues: Whether section 37 of the Mental Health Act 1983 was satisfied on the medical evidence before the Crown Court
What disposal was appropriate on appeal where a hospital order could not stand but immediate release was contested
What further reports were required before final disposal

enrichment.short_title: Serving young offender held homeless for Housing Act purposes despite prison detention

statutes_considered.title: Powers of the Criminal Courts (Sentencing) Act 2000

key_facts: Mr B, aged 17, was serving eight months in a young offender institution and sought accommodation so he could be released on the Home Detention Curfew (tagging) scheme.
Prison Service correspondence made release conditional on securing suitable accommodation before discharge; without it he would remain in custody for the full term.
Southwark Council refused homeless assistance on 2 July 2003 on the basis that lawful detention in prison meant he had accommodation it was reasonable to continue to occupy.
The claimant amended his claim to seek a declaration that he was homeless within Part VII of the Housing Act 1996.
He was in priority need as under 18, but eligibility remained disputed on immigration status despite YOT correspondence about British nationality.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of a local authority decision refusing homelessness assistance to a detained young offender.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration granted that the claimant was homeless within section 175 of the Housing Act 1996 and the 2 July decision was erroneous in law; costs to claimant; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A serving prisoner may be homeless under section 175 of the Housing Act 1996 because prison is not accommodation within Part VII, does not fall within section 175(1)(a)-(c), and it is not reasonable for a prisoner eligible for early release to remain detained solely for lack of accommodation.
legal_issues: Whether detention in a young offender institution constitutes accommodation under section 175
Whether prison accommodation falls within section 175(1)(a), (b) or (c)
Whether it is reasonable under section 175(3) for a curfew-eligible prisoner to continue occupying a prison cell
Budgetary implications for housing authorities

notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment on proprietary estoppel and estoppel by convention in access dispute.

enrichment.short_title: Home Farm access dispute: estoppel upheld over shark's fin right of way
key_facts: Mr Valentine sought to restrain neighbours from crossing land at Jacob's Place (including the 'shark's fin') to reach western plots at a Fulbeck residential development.
Conveyancing plans and Newton plan deeds of grant were incongruous; rights of way had been granted over land not owned by the grantors.
At a July 1991 site meeting Mr Rann and Mr Valentine agreed access on the Newton plan basis; western plot owners built walls and roadways in reliance.
The county court judge declared equitable easements over the shark's fin and shared access land on payment of £6,630, and ordered Valentine to pay damages for obstructing access to plot 1.
The litigation followed incompetent conveyancing by the solicitor who handled the original development transactions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal (permission limited to estoppel and procedural fairness) from Lincoln County Court order of 8 May 2002.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; judge's estoppel findings upheld on proprietary estoppel, personal estoppel, and estoppel by convention grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Where all parties to a residential development acted on the common assumption that access would follow the Newton plan incorporated in the 1991 deeds, estoppel (including estoppel by convention) prevents an owner of land over which access was intended from denying rights inconsistent with that scheme after others acted to their detriment.
legal_issues: Whether the judge procedurally unfairly decided estoppel without adequate pleading of the July 1991 site meeting agreement
Whether proprietary estoppel or estoppel by representation bound Mr Valentine as successor in title
Whether estoppel by convention arose from the shared development scheme
Whether the 1991 deeds of grant were legally effective or only gave rise to equitable rights

notes: Complete patent appeal on obviousness, construction and sufficiency of deep fat fryer patent.

enrichment.short_title: Deep fat fryer patent held obvious despite insulating ring feature

statutes_considered.title: Protocol on the Interpretation of Article 69 of the European Patent Convention

key_facts: SEB SA's patent claimed an electric deep fat fryer with a plastics skirt separated from a hot metal vessel by an air layer, connected by a thermally insulating ring closing the air space.
Pumfrey J held the patent invalid for obviousness but, if valid, infringed De'Longhi's F2, F7 and FP fryer ranges.
The judge found skilled designers in 1987 would naturally use cheap plastics with an insulating ring, drawing on knowledge from kettles, irons and similar appliances.
On construction, 'closes' in claim 1 meant closed enough to prevent practically significant convective escape of hot air, not hermetic sealing.
De'Longhi's spacers and vents did not avoid infringement because airflow was practically negligible.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against High Court dismissal of patent infringement claim on obviousness grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; patent invalid for obviousness in light of common general knowledge; construction and sufficiency points resolved against De'Longhi.
enrichment.ratio: Where common general knowledge in 1987 included double-walled fryers, use of plastics casings, and insulating rings or spacers in heated domestic appliances, applying an insulating ring to enable a cheap polypropylene skirt was an obvious step; 'closes' in the patent claim is purposive and does not require hermetic closure.
legal_issues: Obviousness assessed through the skilled person's eyes using the Windsurfing approach
Whether insulating ring over Taurus prior art involved inventive step
Construction of claim feature requiring the ring to 'close' the air-filled space
Whether De'Longhi fryers would infringe if the patent were valid
Insufficiency of the specification

notes: Full reserved judgment on conviction safety and sentence for hotel room assault.

enrichment.short_title: Hotel strangulation conviction safe despite irregular jury note handling
key_facts: Haja Andriamampandry entered a hotel guest's room at night using a master key and strangled a 22-year-old woman for about ten to thirty seconds before she fought him off.
He pleaded guilty to section 20 grievous bodily harm but denied the section 18 intent required for the indictment on which he was convicted.
At trial he claimed kleptomania and panic when discovered, saying he only sought to silence her.
The judge received 17 written jury notes before retirement; irregularities arose because notes 10 and 13 were not fully read out or shown to defence counsel.
DNA evidence was overwhelming; the jury's questions concerned psychiatric reports and prior thefts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal reserved judgment following appeal against conviction and seven-year sentence from Reading Crown Court (7 December 2001).
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed; sentence appeal allowed and seven years reduced to five years' imprisonment (deportation order unchanged).
enrichment.ratio: Failure to read out or hand jury notes 10 and 13 to counsel was a minor irregularity under R v Gorman principles that did not render the conviction unsafe where the notes could not reasonably have led to a significant additional line of evidence or argument.
legal_issues: Whether irregular handling of jury notes 10, 12 and 13 undermined conviction safety
Application of R v Gorman to pre-retirement jury communications

notes: Full Chancery judgment on ICTA 1988 section 75 expenses of management for abortive takeover costs.

enrichment.short_title: Abortive takeover advisory fees allowed as investment company management expenses
key_facts: Camas Plc, an investment company within ICTA section 130, incurred about £509,695 of professional fees on Project Bardon, an abortive attempt to acquire Bardon Group Plc in 1995.
Fees were paid to Schroders, Warburgs, KPMG, Clifford Chance and others for appraisal, due diligence, takeover documentation and director advice before Bardon rejected a 40p indicative offer.
The Inspector allowed only loan-finance-related fees under section 77; the Special Commissioners held the balance was part of acquisition costs and not expenses of management.
Camas's board needed the advice to decide whether to proceed; much work would have been required even for a hostile bid that was never launched.
If completed, acquisition of Bardon would have been an investment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court (Chancery) appeal on a point of law from Special Commissioners' decision upholding the Inspector's refusal of deduction.
enrichment.outcome: Taxpayer's appeal allowed; abortive Project Bardon professional fees held deductible as expenses of management under section 75.
enrichment.ratio: Professional fees incurred to investigate and decide whether to make a corporate acquisition are severable from the costs of acquisition itself and may be deducted as expenses of management under section 75 even where no purchase completes; capital expenditure may be deducted under section 75 where not already allowable in computing chargeable gains.
legal_issues: Whether abortive takeover fees are expenses of management or part of acquisition costs under the Sun Life test
Whether capital expenditure is deductible under section 75 against total profits
Distinction between appraisal/decision costs and brokerage, stamp duty or success fees
Overlap with TCGA section 38 incidental costs of acquisition

notes: Complete habeas corpus judgment on unjust and oppressive extradition.

enrichment.short_title: Czech extradition refused as unjust and oppressive after long delay
key_facts: The applicant, a Roma from the Czech Republic, was committed at Bow Street on 7 October 2002 to await the Secretary of State's decision on Czech extradition for 1995 offences including living off immoral earnings and theft of vacuum cleaners.
He lived openly in Plzen after charge in February 1996, married in 1998, entered the UK in March 2000 and claimed asylum; Czech authorities issued an arrest warrant only in September 2000.
Alleged immoral earnings involved a 16-year-old persuaded to have paid sexual intercourse with men; vacuum cleaner offences were trivial in value.
The applicant was 19 at the alleged conduct and 27 when extradition was sought; he had a wife, two children and two stepchildren in the UK.
Czech explanations for failure to notify or summon him for trial between 1996 and 1999 were inadequate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court habeas corpus application challenging detention following magistrates' committal for extradition to the Czech Republic.
enrichment.outcome: Habeas corpus granted; extradition would be unjust and oppressive; applicant's costs order for travel granted.
enrichment.ratio: Extradition may be refused under section 11(3) of the Extradition Act 1989 where cumulative delay, the relative triviality of some charges, witness memory concerns, and the dramatic change in the fugitive's personal circumstances make return unjust or oppressive despite lawful committal.
legal_issues: Whether section 11(3) permits refusal on grounds of delay, age and family circumstances
Whether alleged offences were too trivial to justify extradition

notes: Full judicial review on PACE confession definition and Barry section 76 steps.

enrichment.short_title: Customs interview held a PACE confession in VAT carousel committal
key_facts: Mr Theobald, financial director of European Cellular Trading PLC, faced committal for VAT fraud involving missing traders in mobile phone transactions.
District Judge Zara ruled his November 1998 Customs interview was not a confession under section 76 and, alternatively, would have been admitted.
The interview contained admissions adverse to the defendant on knowledge of missing traders, purchase trails and payment approvals relevant to dishonest participation.
Earlier committal had been quashed for procedural irregularity; abuse of process and disclosure issues had a prolonged procedural history.
The defence argued Customs had implied no prosecution would follow; the judge found no such promise.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review (renewed application treated as substantive hearing) of Nottingham magistrates' committal rulings.
enrichment.outcome: Decision that interview was not a confession quashed; declaration that it is a confession; district judge directed to apply R v Barry section 76 steps; full committal to recommence 15 July 2003; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: A police or Customs interview is a confession under section 82 PACE if it contains statements partly adverse to the maker and relied on by the prosecution as true on matters in issue, even without an express admission of guilt; the Barry three-step section 76 analysis must be applied explicitly.
legal_issues: Whether the Customs interview was a confession within section 76 and section 82 PACE
Whether representations via solicitors could be 'something said or done' under section 76(2)(b)
Whether non-confessional hearsay arose if the interview was not a confession
Whether findings that no prosecution promise was made were perverse

notes: Full declaratory judgment on Airports Act 1986 relevant activities and car parking shuttle facilities.

enrichment.short_title: Off-airport shuttle access held outside CAA relevant activities as car parking
key_facts: Airport Parking and Hotels (Birmingham) Ltd operates an off-airport car park near Birmingham International Airport and sought licence terms similar to those offered to Airparks, including 4% turnover fees.
BIA proposed shuttle bus access over airport roads, a terminal lay-by, signage and a courtesy telephone in return for 4% of turnover.
The CAA had upheld a similar complaint by Airparks that 4% turnover was not objectionable under section 41; the OFT also had jurisdiction under competition legislation.
The claimant sought a declaration that shuttle access facilities for off-airport car parking are not 'relevant activities' under sections 36 and 41.
The court held 'airport' means the whole delineated airport undertaking, but section 36(2) excludes facilities for car parking from relevant activities.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review claim for declaratory relief on statutory jurisdiction of the Civil Aviation Authority versus the Office of Fair Trading.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration to be granted that the CAA has no jurisdiction over the claimant's complaint about BIA's proposed 4% turnover licence terms; 80% of claimant's costs ordered; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Shuttle bus access over airport roads with a terminal lay-by, sign and telephone for passengers using an off-airport car park constitutes 'facilities for car parking' excluded from 'relevant activities' by section 36(2) of the Airports Act 1986, so the CAA lacks section 41 jurisdiction and the OFT has exclusive jurisdiction over the competition complaint.
legal_issues: Whether shuttle facilities are provided 'at the airport' within section 36(1)
Whether they are for handling passengers under section 36(1)(c)
Whether section 36(2) excludes off-airport car parking support facilities
Whether 'facilities for car parking' includes lay-by, signage and telephone for a shuttle service
Overlap between CAA and OFT jurisdiction
